questions.q: Which enzyme catalyzes the rate-limiting, committed step of glycolysis?
questions.explain: Phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1) catalyzes the irreversible phosphorylation of fructose 6-phosphate to fructose 1,6-bisphosphate and is the primary rate-limiting enzyme of glycolysis.

open.q: Name the enzyme that catalyzes the rate-limiting, committed step of glycolysis.

questions.q: Which molecule acts as the most potent allosteric activator of hepatic phosphofructokinase-1 during the fed state?
questions.explain: Insulin activates the kinase domain of PFK-2/FBPase-2 to raise fructose 2,6-bisphosphate levels, which strongly activates PFK-1 and stimulates glycolysis.

open.q: Name the molecule that acts as the most potent allosteric activator of hepatic phosphofructokinase-1 during the fed state.

questions.q: How many net ATP molecules are generated per glucose molecule during anaerobic glycolysis?
questions.explain: Anaerobic glycolysis consumes 2 ATP in the preparatory phase and produces 4 ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation in the payoff phase, yielding a net gain of 2 ATP.

open.q: How many net ATP molecules are generated per glucose molecule during anaerobic glycolysis?

questions.q: Which enzyme of glycolysis is inhibited by fluoride ions used in blood glucose collection tubes?
questions.explain: Fluoride forms a magnesium-fluorophosphate complex that inhibits enolase, preventing ex vivo glycolysis and preserving blood glucose levels in sample tubes.

open.q: Name the glycolytic enzyme inhibited by fluoride ions in blood glucose collection tubes.

questions.q: In mature erythrocytes, which enzyme bypasses phosphoglycerate kinase to generate 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate?
questions.explain: The Rapoport-Luebering shunt uses bisphosphoglycerate mutase to convert 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate into 2,3-BPG, which decreases hemoglobin oxygen affinity without net ATP production.

open.q: Name the enzyme in mature erythrocytes that converts 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate into 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate.

questions.q: A 4-year-old boy presents with chronic nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia, splenomegaly, and elevated red cell 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate levels. Deficiency of which glycolytic enzyme explains this presentation?
questions.explain: Pyruvate kinase deficiency impairs ATP generation in mature RBCs, causing rigid membranes and hemolysis while backing up intermediates to elevate 2,3-BPG.

open.q: Deficiency of which glycolytic enzyme causes chronic nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia accompanied by elevated erythrocyte 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate?

questions.q: Unlike hexokinase, hepatic glucokinase has which kinetic property?
questions.explain: Glucokinase (hexokinase IV) has a high Km (low affinity) and high Vmax, allowing the liver to clear high portal glucose loads after a meal without product inhibition by G6P.

open.q: Describe the Km and Vmax characteristics of hepatic glucokinase compared to hexokinase.

questions.q: Arsenate poisoning uncouples substrate-level phosphorylation in glycolysis by substituting for inorganic phosphate in the reaction catalyzed by which enzyme?
questions.explain: Glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase incorporates arsenate instead of Pi to form unstable 1-arseno-3-phosphoglycerate, which spontaneously hydrolyzes without generating ATP.

open.q: Name the glycolytic enzyme whose reaction is uncoupled by arsenate substituting for inorganic phosphate.

questions.q: What is the primary biochemical purpose of reducing pyruvate to lactate during anaerobic glycolysis?
options: Generating extra ATP via lactate dehydrogenase
questions.explain: Lactate dehydrogenase oxidizes NADH back to NAD+, maintaining the NAD+ pool required for glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase to keep glycolysis running.

open.q: State the primary biochemical purpose of converting pyruvate to lactate during anaerobic glycolysis.

questions.q: Which shuttle transfers reducing equivalents from cytosolic NADH into mitochondria without losing ATP yield, producing 2.5 ATP per NADH?
questions.explain: The malate-aspartate shuttle transfers electrons directly to mitochondrial matrix NAD+, entering Complex I to yield ~2.5 ATP per cytosolic NADH in heart and liver.

open.q: Name the shuttle system that transfers reducing equivalents from cytosolic NADH directly to mitochondrial matrix NAD+.

questions.q: Which five cofactors are required by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex?
options: Biotin, pyridoxal phosphate, CoA, FAD, NAD+
questions.explain: The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex requires thiamine pyrophosphate (B1), lipoic acid, coenzyme A (B5), FAD (B2), and NAD+ (B3).

open.q: List the five cofactors required by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex.
accept: Thiamine pyrophosphate, lipoic acid, coenzyme A, FAD, NAD+

questions.q: Which enzyme of the tricarboxylic acid cycle is embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane and participates directly in the electron transport chain?
questions.explain: Succinate dehydrogenase is the only membrane-bound enzyme of the TCA cycle, functioning simultaneously as Complex II of the electron transport chain.

open.q: Name the TCA cycle enzyme that is bound to the inner mitochondrial membrane and forms Complex II of the electron transport chain.

questions.q: How many molecules of NADH, FADH2, and GTP (or ATP) are produced per turn of the TCA cycle from one acetyl-CoA?
questions.explain: One turn of the TCA cycle oxidizes one acetyl-CoA to two CO2 molecules while generating 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, and 1 GTP (via succinyl-CoA synthetase), yielding ~10 ATP.

open.q: State the number of NADH, FADH2, and GTP molecules produced from one acetyl-CoA in a single turn of the TCA cycle.

questions.q: Which compound inhibits aconitase in the TCA cycle after metabolic conversion to fluorocitrate?
questions.explain: Fluoroacetate is converted by citrate synthase into fluorocitrate, a potent suicide inhibitor of aconitase that blocks citrate isomerization to isocitrate.

open.q: Name the toxic compound that is converted into fluorocitrate to inhibit aconitase in the TCA cycle.

questions.q: Which enzyme catalyzes the primary rate-limiting step of the TCA cycle and is allosterically activated by ADP and Ca2+?
questions.explain: Isocitrate dehydrogenase catalyzes the oxidative decarboxylation of isocitrate to alpha-ketoglutarate and is strongly activated by ADP and Ca2+ and inhibited by ATP and NADH.

open.q: Name the primary rate-limiting enzyme of the TCA cycle that is allosterically activated by ADP and calcium ions.

questions.q: A 6-month-old infant presents with severe lactic acidosis, developmental delay, and elevated serum alanine. Treatment includes a ketogenic diet and thiamine supplementation. Which enzyme complex is deficient?
questions.explain: Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex deficiency shunts accumulated pyruvate to lactate and alanine; ketogenic substrates bypass pyruvate to supply acetyl-CoA directly.

open.q: Deficiency of which enzyme complex causes congenital lactic acidosis with elevated alanine that is managed with a ketogenic diet?

questions.q: Which TCA cycle intermediate serves as an allosteric activator of acetyl-CoA carboxylase and an inhibitor of phosphofructokinase-1?
questions.explain: High mitochondrial citrate exits to the cytosol where it signals energy abundance by activating fatty acid synthesis (ACC) and inhibiting glycolysis (PFK-1).

open.q: Name the TCA cycle intermediate that exits mitochondria to activate acetyl-CoA carboxylase and inhibit phosphofructokinase-1.

questions.q: Succinate dehydrogenase is competitively inhibited by which structural analog of succinate?
questions.explain: Malonate closely resembles succinate structurally and binds to the active site of succinate dehydrogenase without undergoing dehydrogenation, acting as a classic competitive inhibitor.

open.q: Name the classic competitive inhibitor of succinate dehydrogenase.

questions.q: Which four enzymes are unique to gluconeogenesis and bypass the three irreversible steps of glycolysis?
options: Pyruvate carboxylase, PEP carboxykinase, fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase, glucose 6-phosphatase
Pyruvate kinase, PEP carboxykinase, PFK-2, glucokinase
Pyruvate dehydrogenase, pyruvate carboxylase, aldolase B, glucose 6-phosphatase
Lactate dehydrogenase, malate dehydrogenase, fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase, hexokinase
questions.explain: Pyruvate carboxylase and PEPCK bypass pyruvate kinase, fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase bypasses PFK-1, and glucose 6-phosphatase bypasses hexokinase/glucokinase.

open.q: Name the four unique enzymes of gluconeogenesis that bypass the three irreversible steps of glycolysis.
accept: Pyruvate carboxylase, PEP carboxykinase, fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase, glucose 6-phosphatase

questions.q: Pyruvate carboxylase requires biotin as a cofactor and is strictly dependent on which allosteric activator?
questions.explain: Acetyl-CoA from fatty acid beta-oxidation is an obligate allosteric activator of pyruvate carboxylase, ensuring oxaloacetate is generated for gluconeogenesis during fasting.

open.q: Name the obligate allosteric activator required for pyruvate carboxylase activity.

questions.q: Why can skeletal muscle not contribute directly to blood glucose maintenance during fasting?
questions.explain: Skeletal muscle lacks glucose 6-phosphatase, so glucose 6-phosphate derived from muscle glycogenolysis cannot be dephosphorylated into free glucose for export.

open.q: Which enzyme is absent in skeletal muscle, preventing it from releasing free glucose into the bloodstream?

questions.q: How many high-energy phosphate bonds (ATP and GTP equivalents) are consumed to synthesize one molecule of glucose from two molecules of pyruvate?
questions.explain: Synthesizing one glucose from two pyruvates consumes 4 ATP (2 at pyruvate carboxylase, 2 at phosphoglycerate kinase) and 2 GTP (2 at PEPCK), totaling 6 high-energy phosphate bonds.

open.q: How many total ATP and GTP equivalents are consumed to synthesize one molecule of glucose from two molecules of pyruvate?

questions.q: In the Cori cycle, lactate produced by exercising skeletal muscle is transported to the liver and converted back into which molecule?
questions.explain: The Cori cycle transfers lactate from anaerobic tissues (muscle, RBCs) to the liver, where gluconeogenesis converts it back into glucose for release into the blood.

open.q: In the Cori cycle, what end product is synthesized in the liver from muscle-derived lactate and returned to the bloodstream?

questions.q: Why are even-chain fatty acids unable to serve as net substrates for gluconeogenesis in humans?
options: They cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane
Their oxidation yields only acetyl-CoA, whose two carbons are lost as CO2 in the TCA cycle
questions.explain: Even-chain fatty acids yield only acetyl-CoA, and because the pyruvate dehydrogenase reaction is irreversible, the two acetyl carbons are lost as CO2 before forming oxaloacetate.

open.q: Explain why even-chain fatty acids cannot provide a net carbon source for gluconeogenesis in humans.
accept: They yield only acetyl-CoA, and the two carbons are lost as CO2 in the TCA cycle
Pyruvate dehydrogenase is irreversible and acetyl-CoA carbons are lost as CO2

questions.q: Which odd-chain fatty acid oxidation product enters the TCA cycle as succinyl-CoA and can contribute to net gluconeogenesis?
questions.explain: Odd-chain fatty acids yield a terminal three-carbon propionyl-CoA, which is converted via methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA, providing net carbons for oxaloacetate and glucose.

open.q: Name the three-carbon product of odd-chain fatty acid oxidation that enters the TCA cycle as succinyl-CoA for gluconeogenesis.

questions.q: Excessive ethanol metabolism inhibits hepatic gluconeogenesis primarily by causing which metabolic shift?
options: Marked increase in the cytosolic NADH/NAD+ ratio
questions.explain: Alcohol and aldehyde dehydrogenases generate excess NADH, shifting lactate dehydrogenase toward lactate and malate dehydrogenase toward malate, depleting pyruvate and oxaloacetate for gluconeogenesis.

open.q: What primary redox shift caused by ethanol oxidation inhibits hepatic gluconeogenesis and triggers fasting hypoglycemia?

questions.q: Which enzyme catalyzes the rate-limiting step of glycogen synthesis by forming alpha-1,4 glycosidic bonds?
questions.explain: Glycogen synthase transfers glucose residues from UDP-glucose to the non-reducing ends of glycogen chains via alpha-1,4 linkages and is the rate-limiting enzyme of glycogenesis.

open.q: Name the rate-limiting enzyme of glycogen synthesis that forms alpha-1,4 glycosidic bonds.

questions.q: What is the primary product released by glycogen phosphorylase during glycogenolysis?
questions.explain: Glycogen phosphorylase uses inorganic phosphate (phosphorolysis) to cleave alpha-1,4 glycosidic bonds, releasing glucose 1-phosphate without consuming ATP.

open.q: Name the phosphorylated sugar released directly by glycogen phosphorylase during glycogen breakdown.

questions.q: Which vitamin-derived cofactor is covalently bound to glycogen phosphorylase and essential for its catalytic activity?
questions.explain: Glycogen phosphorylase requires pyridoxal phosphate (PLP, derived from vitamin B6), whose phosphate group acts as a general acid-base catalyst during phosphorolysis.

open.q: Name the vitamin B6-derived cofactor required by glycogen phosphorylase.

questions.q: During muscle contraction, which ion allosterically activates phosphorylase kinase without requiring cAMP-dependent phosphorylation?
questions.explain: Calcium released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum binds the calmodulin (delta) subunit of muscle phosphorylase kinase, synchronizing glycogenolysis with muscle contraction.

open.q: Name the ion released during muscle contraction that allosterically activates phosphorylase kinase via its calmodulin subunit.

questions.q: A 5-month-old infant presents with severe fasting hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, and hyperlipidemia. Blood glucose fails to rise after glucagon administration. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.explain: Von Gierke disease (Type I glycogen storage disease) is caused by glucose 6-phosphatase deficiency, trapping G6P in the liver and shunting it to glycolysis (lactate), HMP shunt (uric acid), and lipogenesis.

open.q: Deficiency of which enzyme causes Von Gierke disease, characterized by severe fasting hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, lactic acidosis, and hyperuricemia?

questions.q: A 22-year-old man experiences painful muscle cramps and burgundy-colored urine during intense exercise, with a 'second wind' phenomenon after resting and a flat venous lactate curve on ischemic forearm testing. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.explain: McArdle disease (Type V glycogen storage disease) results from skeletal muscle glycogen phosphorylase (myophosphorylase) deficiency, preventing glycogen breakdown during exercise and causing rhabdomyolysis.

open.q: Deficiency of which enzyme causes McArdle disease, presenting with exercise-induced muscle cramps, myoglobinuria, and failure of blood lactate to rise during exercise?

questions.q: Which glycogen storage disease is caused by a lysosomal acid alpha-1,4-glucosidase deficiency and leads to cardiomegaly and early death in infants?
questions.explain: Pompe disease (Type II GSD) is a lysosomal storage disorder caused by acid maltase (acid alpha-1,4-glucosidase) deficiency, leading to massive glycogen accumulation in cardiac and skeletal muscle.

open.q: Name the glycogen storage disease caused by lysosomal acid alpha-1,4-glucosidase deficiency.

questions.q: Which protein acts as a self-glucosylating primer to initiate de novo glycogen synthesis?
questions.explain: Glycogenin attaches the first glucose residues from UDP-glucose onto its own tyrosine hydroxyl group, forming a short oligosaccharide primer extended by glycogen synthase.

open.q: Name the self-glucosylating protein that acts as the primer for de novo glycogen synthesis.

questions.q: How does insulin promote glycogen synthesis in the liver?
options: Activates protein phosphatase-1 to dephosphorylate glycogen synthase
Increases intracellular cAMP to activate protein kinase A
questions.explain: Insulin activates protein phosphatase-1 (PP1), which dephosphorylates and activates glycogen synthase while simultaneously dephosphorylating and inactivating glycogen phosphorylase.

open.q: Which phosphatase is activated by insulin to dephosphorylate and activate glycogen synthase?

questions.sub: Pentose Phosphate Pathway and Monosaccharide Metabolism
questions.q: What are the two major biochemical products of the pentose phosphate pathway?
questions.explain: The pentose phosphate pathway (HMP shunt) generates cytosolic NADPH for reductive biosynthesis and antioxidant defense, as well as ribose 5-phosphate for nucleotide synthesis.

open.q: Name the two primary products generated by the pentose phosphate pathway.

questions.sub: Pentose Phosphate Pathway and Monosaccharide Metabolism
questions.q: Which cofactor is required by transketolase in the non-oxidative phase of the pentose phosphate pathway?
questions.explain: Transketolase transfers two-carbon units between ketose and aldose sugars and strictly requires thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP); erythrocyte transketolase activity is used to assess vitamin B1 status.

open.q: Name the cofactor required by transketolase in the non-oxidative branch of the pentose phosphate pathway.

questions.sub: Pentose Phosphate Pathway and Monosaccharide Metabolism
questions.q: A Nigerian medical student develops acute hemolytic anemia, jaundice, and dark urine two days after taking primaquine for malaria prophylaxis. Peripheral smear shows bite cells and Heinz bodies. Deficiency of which enzyme is responsible?
questions.explain: G6PD deficiency impairs NADPH generation in erythrocytes, preventing glutathione reductase from maintaining reduced glutathione (GSH) to neutralize oxidative stress from antimalarials or fava beans.

open.q: Deficiency of which enzyme leads to primaquine-induced hemolytic anemia with Heinz bodies and bite cells?

questions.sub: Pentose Phosphate Pathway and Monosaccharide Metabolism
questions.q: Why does fructose metabolism in the liver proceed faster than glucose metabolism and bypass key regulatory checkpoints?
options: Fructokinase and aldolase B bypass phosphofructokinase-1
Glucokinase has a higher affinity for fructose than glucose
questions.explain: Hepatic fructokinase phosphorylates fructose to fructose 1-phosphate, which aldolase B cleaves into DHAP and glyceraldehyde, bypassing the rate-limiting PFK-1 step.

open.q: Which rate-limiting glycolytic enzyme is bypassed during hepatic fructose metabolism?

questions.sub: Pentose Phosphate Pathway and Monosaccharide Metabolism
questions.q: A 7-month-old infant develops vomiting, severe hypoglycemia, jaundice, and hepatomegaly shortly after fruit juice and honey are introduced into the diet. Which enzyme deficiency causes this condition?
questions.explain: Hereditary fructose intolerance is caused by aldolase B deficiency, trapping fructose 1-phosphate in hepatocytes and depleting intracellular inorganic phosphate needed for glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.

open.q: What enzyme deficiency causes hereditary fructose intolerance after the introduction of sucrose or fruit into an infant's diet?

questions.sub: Pentose Phosphate Pathway and Monosaccharide Metabolism
questions.q: Classic galactosemia is caused by a deficiency of which enzyme?
questions.explain: Deficiency of galactose 1-phosphate uridylyltransferase (GALT) causes accumulation of toxic galactose 1-phosphate and galactitol, leading to hepatomegaly, jaundice, cataracts, and E. coli neonatal sepsis.

open.q: Name the enzyme whose deficiency causes classic galactosemia.

questions.sub: Pentose Phosphate Pathway and Monosaccharide Metabolism
questions.q: Accumulation of which sugar alcohol in the ocular lens causes cataracts in both galactokinase deficiency and uncontrolled diabetes mellitus?
options: Galactitol and sorbitol via aldose reductase
questions.explain: Aldose reductase reduces excess galactose to galactitol and excess glucose to sorbitol; because lens cells lack sorbitol dehydrogenase and cannot export polyols, osmotic water influx causes cataracts.

open.q: Name the enzyme that reduces excess glucose and galactose into osmotically active polyols in the ocular lens.

questions.sub: Pentose Phosphate Pathway and Monosaccharide Metabolism
questions.q: Which nucleotide sugar serves as the activated donor of glucuronate for bilirubin conjugation and drug detoxification in the liver?
questions.explain: UDP-glucuronic acid, formed via the uronic acid pathway from UDP-glucose, is used by UDP-glucuronosyltransferases to conjugate bilirubin, steroids, and xenobiotics.

open.q: Name the activated nucleotide sugar donor required for glucuronidation of bilirubin and drugs.

questions.sub: Electron Transport Chain and Oxidative Phosphorylation
questions.q: Which component of the electron transport chain is a mobile lipid-soluble quinone that accepts electrons from both Complex I and Complex II?
questions.explain: Coenzyme Q (ubiquinone) diffuses freely within the inner mitochondrial membrane, collecting electrons from Complexes I and II (as well as ETF and glycerol 3-phosphate dehydrogenase) and passing them to Complex III.

open.q: Name the mobile lipid-soluble electron carrier that transfers electrons from Complexes I and II to Complex III.

questions.sub: Electron Transport Chain and Oxidative Phosphorylation
questions.q: Which electron transport chain complex transfers electrons directly to molecular oxygen to form water?
questions.explain: Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) contains heme a, heme a3, CuA, and CuB centers that catalyze the four-electron reduction of O2 to two molecules of H2O.

open.q: Name the electron transport chain complex that reduces molecular oxygen to water.

questions.sub: Electron Transport Chain and Oxidative Phosphorylation
questions.q: Cyanide and carbon monoxide inhibit oxidative phosphorylation by binding to which specific component?
questions.explain: Cyanide (binds Fe3+) and carbon monoxide (binds Fe2+) inhibit Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase), halting electron transfer to oxygen and collapsing the proton gradient.

open.q: Which enzyme complex of the electron transport chain is inhibited by cyanide and carbon monoxide?

questions.sub: Electron Transport Chain and Oxidative Phosphorylation
questions.q: How do uncoupling agents such as 2,4-dinitrophenol and thermogenin (UCP1) affect oxygen consumption and ATP synthesis?
options: Increase oxygen consumption, decrease ATP synthesis, and generate heat
Decrease both oxygen consumption and ATP synthesis
Increase both oxygen consumption and ATP synthesis
Inhibit Complex I while stimulating ATP synthase
questions.explain: Uncouplers dissipate the proton-motive force across the inner mitochondrial membrane by allowing protons to re-enter the matrix without passing through ATP synthase, releasing energy as heat while electron transport accelerates.

open.q: Describe the effect of uncoupling agents like 2,4-dinitrophenol on oxygen consumption, ATP synthesis, and heat production.
accept: Increase oxygen consumption and heat production while decreasing ATP synthesis
Increase O2 consumption, decrease ATP, increase heat

questions.sub: Electron Transport Chain and Oxidative Phosphorylation
questions.q: Which antibiotic inhibits oxidative phosphorylation by directly blocking the proton channel (Fo subunit) of ATP synthase?
questions.explain: Oligomycin binds the Fo subunit of ATP synthase, blocking proton reentry into the matrix; because the proton gradient builds up to a maximum, electron transport also stops unless an uncoupler is added.

open.q: Name the antibiotic that inhibits oxidative phosphorylation by blocking the Fo proton channel of ATP synthase.

questions.sub: Electron Transport Chain and Oxidative Phosphorylation
questions.q: Which poison inhibits Complex I (NADH-coenzyme Q oxidoreductase) of the electron transport chain?
questions.explain: Rotenone (a plant-derived insecticide) and barbiturates like amobarbital block electron transfer from the iron-sulfur centers of Complex I to ubiquinone.

open.q: Name the insecticide poison that inhibits Complex I of the electron transport chain.

questions.sub: Electron Transport Chain and Oxidative Phosphorylation
questions.q: In brown adipose tissue of newborns, which hormone stimulates lipolysis to provide free fatty acids that activate thermogenin (UCP1) for non-shivering thermogenesis?
questions.explain: Cold exposure triggers sympathetic release of norepinephrine onto beta-3 adrenergic receptors in brown fat, activating hormone-sensitive lipase; released fatty acids activate UCP1 to generate heat.

open.q: Name the catecholamine hormone that stimulates brown adipose tissue to activate thermogenin (UCP1) during cold exposure.

questions.q: Which enzyme catalyzes the rate-limiting step of de novo fatty acid synthesis?
questions.explain: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) catalyzes the biotin-dependent carboxylation of acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA and is the primary regulated step in fatty acid synthesis.

open.q: Name the rate-limiting enzyme of de novo fatty acid synthesis.

questions.q: How does AMPK (AMP-activated protein kinase) regulate acetyl-CoA carboxylase during fasting or energy depletion?
questions.explain: During low energy states (high AMP/ATP) or glucagon signaling, AMPK phosphorylates acetyl-CoA carboxylase, inactivating it to stop fatty acid synthesis and relieve malonyl-CoA inhibition of CPT-I.

open.q: What is the effect of AMPK-mediated phosphorylation on acetyl-CoA carboxylase activity?

questions.q: How is mitochondrial acetyl-CoA transported into the cytosol for fatty acid synthesis?
options: By direct diffusion across the inner membrane
As citrate via the tricarboxylate transporter
questions.explain: Acetyl-CoA condenses with oxaloacetate to form citrate, which exits the mitochondria and is cleaved by cytosolic ATP-citrate lyase back into acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate.

open.q: In what molecular form is mitochondrial acetyl-CoA exported to the cytosol for fatty acid synthesis?

questions.q: Which two cytosolic pathways supply the NADPH required by fatty acid synthase to synthesize palmitate?
options: Pentose phosphate pathway and malic enzyme
questions.explain: The oxidative branch of the pentose phosphate pathway and cytosolic NADP+-dependent malic enzyme (converting malate to pyruvate) generate the NADPH required for reductive fatty acid synthesis.

open.q: Name the two cytosolic sources of NADPH used during de novo fatty acid synthesis.
accept: Pentose phosphate pathway and malic enzyme

questions.q: What is the primary 16-carbon saturated fatty acid end product released by mammalian fatty acid synthase?
questions.explain: Mammalian fatty acid synthase sequentially adds two-carbon units from malonyl-CoA until thioesterase cleaves the 16-carbon saturated fatty acid palmitate.

open.q: Name the 16-carbon saturated fatty acid released as the primary product of mammalian fatty acid synthase.

questions.q: Why are linoleic acid and alpha-linolenic acid essential fatty acids in humans?
options: Humans cannot introduce double bonds beyond carbon-9 from the carboxyl end
They cannot be absorbed without bile salts
They are required to synthesize cholesterol
questions.explain: Human desaturases can only introduce double bonds at positions delta-4, delta-5, delta-6, and delta-9, so omega-6 (linoleic) and omega-3 (alpha-linolenic) fatty acids must be obtained from the diet.

open.q: Explain biochemically why linoleic acid and alpha-linolenic acid are essential fatty acids in humans.
accept: Humans lack desaturases capable of introducing double bonds beyond carbon 9

questions.q: Which molecule inhibits carnitine palmitoyltransferase I (CPT-I) to prevent simultaneous fatty acid synthesis and beta-oxidation?
questions.explain: Malonyl-CoA, the product of acetyl-CoA carboxylase, allosterically inhibits CPT-I on the outer mitochondrial membrane, preventing newly synthesized fatty acids from entering mitochondria for oxidation.

open.q: Name the intermediate of fatty acid synthesis that inhibits carnitine palmitoyltransferase I.

questions.q: What are the four repeating enzymatic steps of mitochondrial beta-oxidation in exact chronological order?
questions.explain: Each cycle of beta-oxidation consists of FAD-linked oxidation (acyl-CoA dehydrogenase), hydration (enoyl-CoA hydratase), NAD+-linked oxidation (3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase), and thiolysis (beta-ketothiolase).

open.q: State the four enzymatic steps of one cycle of mitochondrial beta-oxidation in chronological order.

questions.q: How many net ATP molecules are generated from the complete oxidation of one molecule of palmitoyl-CoA (C16)?
questions.explain: Palmitoyl-CoA undergoes 7 cycles of beta-oxidation yielding 7 FADH2 (10.5 ATP), 7 NADH (17.5 ATP), and 8 acetyl-CoA (80 ATP), totaling 108 ATP (or 106 net ATP starting from free palmitate due to 2 ATP equivalents used for activation).

open.q: How many ATP molecules are produced from the complete mitochondrial oxidation of one molecule of already-activated palmitoyl-CoA?

questions.q: A 10-month-old infant presents with severe hypoketotic hypoglycemia, lethargy, and vomiting after a 14-hour overnight fast during a viral illness. Urine organic acids show elevated C6-C10 dicarboxylic acids. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.explain: MCAD deficiency impairs mitochondrial beta-oxidation of medium-chain fatty acids during fasting, depleting acetyl-CoA needed for ketogenesis and gluconeogenesis while shunting fatty acids to omega-oxidation (dicarboxylic aciduria).

open.q: Deficiency of which enzyme causes fasting hypoketotic hypoglycemia with medium-chain dicarboxylic aciduria?

questions.q: Where does alpha-oxidation of branched-chain fatty acids such as phytanic acid occur, and what disorder results from its defect?
questions.explain: Phytanic acid has a methyl group on its beta-carbon that blocks beta-oxidation; peroxisomal phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase performs alpha-oxidation, and its deficiency causes Refsum disease (retinitis pigmentosa, peripheral neuropathy, ataxia).

open.q: Name the organelle where alpha-oxidation of phytanic acid occurs and the disorder caused by its deficiency.

questions.q: Which enzyme catalyzes the rate-limiting step of hepatic ketogenesis?
questions.explain: Mitochondrial HMG-CoA synthase condenses acetoacetyl-CoA with acetyl-CoA to form HMG-CoA and is the rate-limiting enzyme of ketogenesis.

open.q: Name the rate-limiting enzyme of hepatic ketogenesis.

questions.q: Why is the liver unable to utilize the ketone bodies it synthesizes as an energy source?
options: Ketone bodies cannot cross the hepatocyte plasma membrane
questions.explain: The liver lacks succinyl-CoA:acetoacetate CoA transferase (thiophorase), ensuring that all synthesized ketone bodies are exported to extrahepatic tissues like brain, heart, and skeletal muscle.

open.q: Name the enzyme absent in hepatocytes that prevents the liver from utilizing ketone bodies as fuel.

questions.q: In diabetic ketoacidosis, why does the standard urine nitroprusside test underestimate total ketone body concentration?
options: It detects acetoacetate and acetone, but does not react with beta-hydroxybutyrate
High glucose interferes with the nitroprusside reagent
Beta-hydroxybutyrate is not excreted in urine
questions.explain: The high NADH/NAD+ ratio in DKA favors reduction of acetoacetate to beta-hydroxybutyrate, which lacks a ketone group and therefore does not react with nitroprusside.

open.q: Which predominant ketone body in diabetic ketoacidosis is not detected by the standard nitroprusside test?

questions.q: Which enzyme catalyzes the rate-limiting step of cholesterol biosynthesis and is inhibited by statins?
questions.explain: HMG-CoA reductase converts HMG-CoA to mevalonate using two NADPH molecules and is the primary regulatory and pharmacologic target in cholesterol synthesis.

open.q: Name the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis that is competitively inhibited by statin drugs.

questions.q: How does high intracellular cholesterol suppress de novo cholesterol synthesis at the transcriptional level?
options: Activates LXR to transcribe HMG-CoA reductase
Retains the SCAP-SREBP-2 complex in the endoplasmic reticulum
questions.explain: When sterol levels are high, Insig binds SCAP and anchors the SCAP-SREBP-2 complex in the ER membrane, preventing SREBP-2 proteolytic activation in the Golgi and halting HMG-CoA reductase and LDL receptor transcription.

open.q: Explain how high intracellular cholesterol prevents SREBP-2 from activating transcription of HMG-CoA reductase.
accept: Cholesterol promotes Insig binding to SCAP, retaining the SCAP-SREBP-2 complex in the endoplasmic reticulum
Retains SCAP-SREBP complex in the ER

questions.q: Which enzyme catalyzes the rate-limiting step in the synthesis of primary bile acids from cholesterol?
questions.explain: Cholesterol 7-alpha-hydroxylase (CYP7A1) catalyzes the rate-limiting step of bile acid synthesis; it is upregulated by cholesterol and feedback-inhibited by bile acids.

open.q: Name the rate-limiting enzyme of primary bile acid synthesis.

questions.q: Which apolipoprotein activates lipoprotein lipase (LPL) on capillary endothelium to hydrolyze triglycerides in chylomicrons and VLDL?
questions.explain: Apolipoprotein C-II, transferred from HDL to nascent chylomicrons and VLDL, is an obligate cofactor that activates capillary lipoprotein lipase.

open.q: Name the apolipoprotein that acts as a cofactor to activate capillary lipoprotein lipase.

questions.q: Which apolipoprotein activates lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase (LCAT) to esterify free cholesterol on HDL?
questions.explain: Apolipoprotein A-I is the major structural protein of HDL and activates LCAT, converting nascent discoidal HDL into mature spherical HDL3 and HDL2.

open.q: Name the apolipoprotein on HDL that activates lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase (LCAT).

questions.q: A 28-year-old man presents with tendon xanthomas on his Achilles tendons, xanthelasma, and a serum LDL cholesterol of 340 mg/dL. His father died of a myocardial infarction at age 38. What is the primary molecular defect?
questions.explain: Familial hypercholesterolemia (Type IIa hyperlipoproteinemia) is most commonly an autosomal dominant loss-of-function mutation in the LDL receptor gene, impairing hepatic LDL clearance.

open.q: What is the primary molecular defect in autosomal dominant familial hypercholesterolemia?
accept: Mutation in the LDL receptor gene

questions.q: Abetalipoproteinemia is caused by a mutation in microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTP), preventing the assembly of which two lipoproteins?
questions.explain: MTP is required to load triglycerides onto ApoB-48 in enterocytes and ApoB-100 in hepatocytes; its absence leads to fat malabsorption, acanthocytosis, and fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies.

open.q: Which two lipoproteins fail to be assembled and secreted in abetalipoproteinemia?

questions.q: Which enzyme mediates the transfer of cholesteryl esters from HDL to VLDL and LDL in exchange for triglycerides?
questions.explain: Cholesteryl ester transfer protein (CETP) exchanges cholesteryl esters from HDL for triglycerides from VLDL, IDL, and LDL during reverse cholesterol transport.

open.q: Name the plasma protein that transfers cholesteryl esters from HDL to VLDL and LDL in exchange for triglycerides.

questions.q: Which phospholipid is the primary surface-active component of pulmonary surfactant that prevents alveolar collapse?
questions.explain: Dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC / lecithin) lowers alveolar surface tension; a lecithin-to-sphingomyelin (L/S) ratio greater than 2.0 in amniotic fluid indicates fetal lung maturity.

open.q: Name the major phospholipid component of pulmonary surfactant responsible for lowering alveolar surface tension.

questions.q: Which unique phospholipid is located almost exclusively in the inner mitochondrial membrane and is essential for respiratory chain stability?
questions.explain: Cardiolipin (diphosphatidylglycerol) is synthesized from phosphatidylglycerol and CDP-diacylglycerol in the inner mitochondrial membrane, where it stabilizes electron transport complexes.

open.q: Name the diphosphatidylglycerol phospholipid enriched in the inner mitochondrial membrane.

questions.q: A 9-month-old infant presents with developmental regression, hyperacusis, and a cherry-red spot on the macula without hepatosplenomegaly. Deficiency of which lysosomal enzyme causes this disorder?
questions.explain: Tay-Sachs disease is caused by hexosaminidase A deficiency, resulting in GM2 ganglioside accumulation in neurons, neurodegeneration, and a macular cherry-red spot without organomegaly (unlike Niemann-Pick disease).

open.q: Deficiency of which lysosomal enzyme causes Tay-Sachs disease?

questions.q: A 14-year-old boy presents with pancytopenia, massive hepatosplenomegaly, and bone pain. Bone marrow biopsy shows macrophages with a 'crinkled tissue paper' cytoplasm. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.explain: Gaucher disease is the most common lysosomal storage disease, caused by beta-glucocerebrosidase deficiency leading to glucocerebroside accumulation in Gaucher macrophages.

open.q: Deficiency of which lysosomal enzyme causes Gaucher disease?

questions.q: Corticosteroids inhibit the synthesis of both prostaglandins and leukotrienes primarily by inducing lipocortin (annexin A1) to block which enzyme?
questions.explain: Phospholipase A2 cleaves arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids; corticosteroids induce annexin A1 to inhibit PLA2, shutting down both COX and LOX eicosanoid pathways.

open.q: Name the enzyme inhibited by corticosteroid-induced annexin A1 to prevent arachidonic acid release from membrane phospholipids.

questions.q: How does low-dose aspirin exert its cardioprotective antiplatelet effect?
options: Blocks ADP P2Y12 receptors on platelets
Irreversibly acetylates platelet COX-1 to prevent thromboxane A2 synthesis
questions.explain: Aspirin irreversibly acetylates a serine residue in COX-1; because platelets lack nuclei and cannot synthesize new COX-1, thromboxane A2 production is blocked for the lifespan of the platelet.

open.q: Explain the mechanism by which low-dose aspirin inhibits platelet aggregation.
accept: Irreversibly acetylates and inhibits platelet COX-1, blocking thromboxane A2 synthesis

questions.sub: Amino Acid Catabolism and Urea Cycle
questions.q: Which cofactor is required by all aminotransferases (transaminases) such as ALT and AST?
questions.explain: Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP, from vitamin B6) forms a Schiff base with the alpha-amino group of amino acids during transamination reactions.

open.q: Name the vitamin B6-derived cofactor required by all aminotransferases.

questions.sub: Amino Acid Catabolism and Urea Cycle
questions.q: Which enzyme catalyzes the oxidative deamination of glutamate to release free ammonium ions in hepatocyte mitochondria?
questions.explain: Glutamate dehydrogenase uses either NAD+ or NADP+ to convert glutamate into alpha-ketoglutarate and free NH4+, funneling amino nitrogen into the urea cycle.

open.q: Name the mitochondrial enzyme that catalyzes the oxidative deamination of glutamate to alpha-ketoglutarate and free ammonia.

questions.sub: Amino Acid Catabolism and Urea Cycle
questions.q: Which two amino acids serve as the primary non-toxic carriers of ammonia from peripheral tissues and skeletal muscle to the liver?
questions.explain: Glutamine transports nitrogen from most peripheral tissues (via glutamine synthetase), while alanine carries nitrogen from skeletal muscle to the liver via the glucose-alanine (Cahill) cycle.

open.q: Name the two amino acids that act as the major non-toxic transport forms of ammonia from peripheral tissues to the liver.

questions.sub: Amino Acid Catabolism and Urea Cycle
questions.q: What are the two direct nitrogen donors for the two nitrogen atoms of a urea molecule?
questions.explain: One nitrogen of urea enters as free NH4+ (incorporated into carbamoyl phosphate by CPS-I), and the second nitrogen is donated directly by aspartate (in the argininosuccinate synthetase step).

open.q: Name the two direct nitrogen donors that supply the two nitrogen atoms of urea.

questions.sub: Amino Acid Catabolism and Urea Cycle
questions.q: Which enzyme catalyzes the rate-limiting step of the urea cycle and requires N-acetylglutamate as an obligate allosteric activator?
questions.explain: Mitochondrial carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS-I) is the rate-limiting enzyme of the urea cycle and is strictly inactive without N-acetylglutamate (NAG).

open.q: Name the rate-limiting enzyme of the urea cycle and its obligate allosteric activator.
accept: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I and N-acetylglutamate

questions.sub: Amino Acid Catabolism and Urea Cycle
questions.q: A 3-day-old male neonate develops lethargy, vomiting, tachypnea with respiratory alkalosis, and severe hyperammonemia. Urine organic acid analysis shows markedly elevated orotic acid, while plasma citrulline is low. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.explain: Ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency is an X-linked urea cycle disorder; accumulated mitochondrial carbamoyl phosphate leaks into the cytosol and enters pyrimidine synthesis, causing orotic aciduria.

open.q: Deficiency of which X-linked urea cycle enzyme causes hyperammonemia accompanied by elevated urinary orotic acid?

questions.sub: Amino Acid Catabolism and Urea Cycle
questions.q: Why does hyperammonemia cause severe neurotoxicity and cerebral edema?
options: Ammonia consumes alpha-ketoglutarate and raises astrocytic glutamine, impairing energy metabolism and causing swelling
questions.explain: High ammonia drives glutamate dehydrogenase and glutamine synthetase forward in astrocytes, depleting TCA cycle alpha-ketoglutarate and accumulating osmotically active glutamine.

open.q: Explain the metabolic mechanism by which hyperammonemia depletes ATP and causes astrocyte swelling in the brain.
accept: Excess ammonia consumes alpha-ketoglutarate to form glutamate and osmotically active glutamine
Depletion of alpha-ketoglutarate and accumulation of glutamine in astrocytes

questions.sub: Amino Acid Catabolism and Urea Cycle
questions.q: Which two amino acids are exclusively ketogenic?
questions.explain: Leucine and lysine are purely ketogenic, degrading exclusively into acetyl-CoA and acetoacetate without generating any glucogenic intermediates.

open.q: Name the two amino acids that are strictly ketogenic.

questions.sub: Amino Acid Catabolism and Urea Cycle
questions.q: A 6-month-old infant with fair skin, blue eyes, and a musty body odor exhibits severe intellectual disability. Deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase or which cofactor causes this condition?
questions.explain: Classic phenylketonuria (PKU) is caused by phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency, while malignant PKU results from deficiency of its cofactor tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) or dihydropteridine reductase.

open.q: Name the cofactor required by phenylalanine hydroxylase whose deficiency causes malignant phenylketonuria.

questions.sub: Amino Acid Catabolism and Urea Cycle
questions.q: A 35-year-old man presents with dark blue-black pigmentation of his ear cartilage and sclerae, severe lumbar arthritis, and urine that turns black upon standing. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.explain: Alkaptonuria is an autosomal recessive deficiency of homogentisate oxidase in the tyrosine catabolic pathway; homogentisic acid oxidizes to a black polymer (ochronosis) in urine and connective tissues.

open.q: Deficiency of which enzyme in tyrosine metabolism causes alkaptonuria and ochronosis?

questions.sub: Amino Acid Catabolism and Urea Cycle
questions.q: A 5-day-old neonate presents with poor feeding, lethargy, dystonia, and urine with a sweet, burnt-sugar odor. Which enzyme complex is deficient?
questions.explain: Maple syrup urine disease (MSUD) results from branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase deficiency, causing accumulation of leucine, isoleucine, valine, and their alpha-ketoacids.

open.q: Deficiency of which enzyme complex causes maple syrup urine disease?

questions.sub: Amino Acid Catabolism and Urea Cycle
questions.q: Homocystinuria caused by cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency is often treated with high doses of which vitamin cofactor?
questions.explain: Cystathionine beta-synthase requires pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6) to condense homocysteine with serine into cystathionine; vitamin B6 supplementation increases residual enzyme activity in responsive patients.

open.q: Name the vitamin cofactor required by cystathionine beta-synthase that is used to treat responsive patients with homocystinuria.

questions.q: Which amino acid serves as the precursor for niacin (vitamin B3), serotonin, and melatonin?
questions.explain: Tryptophan is hydroxylated and decarboxylated to serotonin (and subsequently melatonin), and is also metabolized via the kynurenine pathway to synthesize NAD+ (niacin).

open.q: Name the essential amino acid precursor of serotonin, melatonin, and endogenous niacin.

questions.q: Which three amino acids are required to synthesize creatine?
questions.explain: Glycine and arginine form guanidinoacetate in the kidney, which is then methylated in the liver by S-adenosylmethionine (from methionine) to form creatine.

open.q: Name the three amino acids required for the biosynthesis of creatine.

questions.q: What is the tripeptide sequence of reduced glutathione (GSH)?
questions.explain: Glutathione is an atypical tripeptide composed of glutamate (linked via its gamma-carboxyl group), cysteine (providing the active thiol group), and glycine.

open.q: Name the three constituent amino acids of glutathione.

questions.q: Which enzyme converts norepinephrine into epinephrine in the adrenal medulla and is induced by cortisol?
questions.explain: Phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase (PNMT) uses S-adenosylmethionine to methylate norepinephrine to epinephrine and is transcriptionally upregulated by high local cortisol from the adrenal cortex.

open.q: Name the SAM-dependent enzyme that methylates norepinephrine to epinephrine in the adrenal medulla.

questions.q: Which two starting substrates condense in the rate-limiting first step of heme synthesis?
questions.explain: Mitochondrial delta-aminolevulinic acid synthase (ALAS) condenses glycine and succinyl-CoA using pyridoxal phosphate to form delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA).

open.q: Name the two substrates condensed by ALA synthase in the rate-limiting step of heme biosynthesis.

questions.q: Which two enzymes of heme biosynthesis are inhibited by lead poisoning?
questions.explain: Lead inhibits cytoplasmic ALA dehydratase (causing elevated delta-ALA) and mitochondrial ferrochelatase (causing elevated erythrocyte protoporphyrin and sideroblastic anemia).

open.q: Name the two enzymes in the heme biosynthetic pathway that are inhibited by lead.

questions.q: A 26-year-old woman presents with severe episodic abdominal pain, peripheral neuropathy, and psychosis triggered by phenobarbital use. Her urine turns port-wine colored upon exposure to light, without photosensitivity skin lesions. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.explain: Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) is caused by porphobilinogen deaminase (hydroxymethylbilane synthase) deficiency; barbiturates induce hepatic CYP450 and ALAS1, accumulating neurotoxic ALA and PBG without cutaneous photosensitivity.

open.q: Deficiency of which enzyme causes acute intermittent porphyria?

questions.q: Which porphyria is the most common, presents with painless blistering skin lesions on sun-exposed hands, and is caused by uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency?
questions.explain: Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) results from uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency, causing accumulation of photoreactive uroporphyrins that produce tea-colored urine and blistering photosensitivity.

open.q: Name the most common porphyria, characterized by blistering photosensitivity and caused by uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency.

questions.q: During heme degradation in macrophages, heme oxygenase cleaves the porphyrin ring to yield biliverdin, ferrous iron, and which gaseous byproduct?
questions.explain: Heme oxygenase oxidatively cleaves the alpha-methene bridge of heme, releasing Fe2+, biliverdin, and carbon monoxide (the sole endogenous source of CO in the human body).

open.q: Name the gas released alongside biliverdin and iron when heme oxygenase degrades heme.

questions.q: A 19-year-old medical student notices mild scleral icterus during exam week fasting, with an isolated unconjugated bilirubin of 2.6 mg/dL and normal liver enzymes and reticulocyte count. Which enzyme has reduced activity?
questions.explain: Gilbert syndrome is a benign autosomal recessive promoter polymorphism reducing hepatic UDP-glucuronosyltransferase 1A1 (UGT1A1) activity, causing mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia during fasting or stress.

open.q: Reduced activity of which hepatic conjugating enzyme causes Gilbert syndrome?

questions.q: Which activated sugar provides the ribose-phosphate backbone for both de novo purine synthesis and salvage pathways?
questions.explain: 5-phosphoribosyl-1-pyrophosphate (PRPP), synthesized from ribose 5-phosphate and ATP by PRPP synthetase, is required for both de novo purine/pyrimidine synthesis and purine salvage.

open.q: Name the activated ribose donor required for both de novo nucleotide synthesis and purine salvage pathways.

questions.q: Which enzyme catalyzes the committed, rate-limiting step of de novo purine biosynthesis?
questions.explain: Glutamine-PRPP amidotransferase replaces the pyrophosphate of PRPP with the amide nitrogen of glutamine to form 5-phosphoribosylamine and is feedback-inhibited by IMP, AMP, and GMP.

open.q: Name the enzyme that catalyzes the committed step of de novo purine nucleotide synthesis.

questions.q: Which three amino acids donate carbon and nitrogen atoms directly to the purine ring during de novo synthesis?
questions.explain: The purine ring atoms are derived from glycine (C4, C5, N7), aspartate (N1), glutamine amide nitrogen (N3, N9), N10-formyl-THF (C2, C8), and CO2 (C6).

open.q: Name the three amino acids that contribute atoms directly to the purine ring during de novo synthesis.

questions.q: A 2-year-old boy presents with developmental delay, spasticity, severe self-mutilating biting of his lips and fingers, and orange crystals in his diaper. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.explain: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is an X-linked deficiency of HGPRT, preventing salvage of hypoxanthine and guanine, causing PRPP accumulation, accelerated de novo purine synthesis, hyperuricemia, and self-mutilation.

open.q: Deficiency of which purine salvage enzyme causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome?

questions.q: Deficiency of adenosine deaminase causes severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) primarily because accumulation of which toxic metabolite inhibits ribonucleotide reductase in lymphocytes?
questions.explain: Adenosine deaminase deficiency leads to massive buildup of deoxyadenosine and dATP in T and B lymphocytes; dATP allosterically inhibits ribonucleotide reductase, halting DNA synthesis.

open.q: Name the deoxynucleotide that accumulates in adenosine deaminase deficiency and allosterically inhibits ribonucleotide reductase.

questions.q: Which molybdenum- and iron-containing enzyme oxidizes hypoxanthine to xanthine and xanthine to uric acid?
questions.explain: Xanthine oxidase catalyzes the final two oxidation steps of purine catabolism to uric acid and is inhibited by allopurinol and febuxostat in the treatment of gout.

open.q: Name the enzyme inhibited by allopurinol that converts hypoxanthine and xanthine into uric acid.

questions.q: Which enzyme catalyzes the rate-limiting step of de novo pyrimidine synthesis in the cytosol?
questions.explain: Cytosolic carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II (CPS-II) uses glutamine, CO2, and 2 ATP to form carbamoyl phosphate for pyrimidine synthesis and is inhibited by UTP and activated by PRPP.

open.q: Name the cytosolic enzyme that catalyzes the rate-limiting step of de novo pyrimidine biosynthesis.

questions.q: Which enzyme converts dUMP to dTMP using N5,N10-methylenetetrahydrofolate as both a one-carbon donor and a reducing agent?
questions.explain: Thymidylate synthase methylates dUMP to dTMP while oxidizing N5,N10-methylene-THF to dihydrofolate (DHF); it is irreversibly inhibited by 5-fluorouracil (via FdUMP).

open.q: Name the enzyme that converts dUMP to dTMP and is inhibited by 5-fluorouracil.

questions.q: Hereditary orotic aciduria (characterized by megaloblastic anemia unresponsive to vitamin B12 or folate and crystalluria without hyperammonemia) is caused by a defect in which enzyme?
questions.explain: UMP synthase is a bifunctional enzyme (orotate phosphoribosyltransferase and OMP decarboxylase); its deficiency impairs pyrimidine synthesis and is treated with oral uridine.

open.q: Deficiency of which bifunctional pyrimidine synthesis enzyme causes hereditary orotic aciduria?

questions.q: Which protein supplies electrons directly to ribonucleotide reductase for the conversion of ribonucleoside diphosphates to deoxyribonucleoside diphosphates?
questions.explain: Thioredoxin provides the reducing equivalents (via two cysteine thiol groups) to ribonucleotide reductase and is subsequently regenerated by NADPH-dependent thioredoxin reductase.

open.q: Name the small redox protein that donates reducing equivalents directly to ribonucleotide reductase.

questions.sub: Metabolic Integration: Fed, Fasting, and Starvation States
questions.q: Which GLUT transporter is insulin-dependent and translocates to the plasma membrane in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue after a meal?
questions.explain: Insulin signaling via PI3K/Akt promotes fusion of intracellular GLUT4-containing vesicles with the sarcolemma and adipocyte membrane to increase glucose uptake.

open.q: Name the insulin-responsive glucose transporter expressed in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue.

questions.sub: Metabolic Integration: Fed, Fasting, and Starvation States
questions.q: Which bidirectional, low-affinity glucose transporter is expressed in hepatocytes and pancreatic beta-cells to act as a glucose sensor?
questions.explain: GLUT2 has a high Km (~15-20 mM), allowing glucose entry into pancreatic beta-cells and hepatocytes to scale proportionally with postprandial blood glucose concentrations.

open.q: Name the high-Km glucose transporter found in pancreatic beta-cells and hepatocytes.

questions.sub: Metabolic Integration: Fed, Fasting, and Starvation States
questions.q: Between 12 and 24 hours of fasting, which metabolic pathway becomes the predominant source of blood glucose as hepatic glycogen stores become depleted?
questions.explain: Hepatic glycogen reserves are largely exhausted within 18-24 hours of fasting, making hepatic (and later renal) gluconeogenesis from lactate, glycerol, and alanine the primary source of blood glucose.

open.q: Which metabolic pathway becomes the primary source of blood glucose after 24 hours of fasting?

questions.sub: Metabolic Integration: Fed, Fasting, and Starvation States
questions.q: During prolonged starvation (beyond 3 days), how does the brain adapt to preserve skeletal muscle protein?
options: Switches to direct oxidation of long-chain fatty acids
Increases anaerobic glycolysis using muscle glycogen
Uses branched-chain amino acids directly as its primary fuel
Derives up to two-thirds of its energy from ketone bodies
questions.explain: The brain cannot oxidize fatty acids directly due to the blood-brain barrier, so it upregulates ketolytic enzymes to burn beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate, reducing hepatic gluconeogenesis and muscle proteolysis.

open.q: How does the human brain adapt its fuel utilization during prolonged starvation to spare skeletal muscle protein?
accept: It uses ketone bodies for the majority of its energy needs

questions.sub: Metabolic Integration: Fed, Fasting, and Starvation States
questions.q: Which enzyme in adipose tissue is phosphorylated and activated by protein kinase A in response to glucagon and epinephrine to hydrolyze stored triglycerides?
questions.explain: Catecholamines (and glucagon in some species) elevate cAMP and activate PKA, which phosphorylates hormone-sensitive lipase and perilipin to mobilize free fatty acids and glycerol from adipocytes.

open.q: Name the intracellular adipocyte lipase activated via cAMP/PKA phosphorylation to mobilize stored triglycerides during fasting.

questions.sub: Metabolic Integration: Fed, Fasting, and Starvation States
questions.q: A malnourished patient with chronic alcohol use disorder receives rapid high-dose parenteral glucose without thiamine supplementation and develops acute confusion, ophthalmoplegia, and ataxia. Which metabolic crisis has been precipitated?
questions.explain: Administering glucose before thiamine rapidly exhausts remaining thiamine pyrophosphate stores via pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, precipitating acute Wernicke encephalopathy.

open.q: Name the acute neurological disorder precipitated by administering glucose before thiamine in a thiamine-deficient patient.

questions.q: Which glycolytic enzyme catalyzes the first substrate-level phosphorylation step, generating ATP from 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate?
questions.explain: Phosphoglycerate kinase transfers the high-energy acyl phosphate from 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate to ADP, forming 3-phosphoglycerate and the first ATP of glycolysis.

open.q: Name the glycolytic enzyme that catalyzes the transfer of a phosphate group from 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate to ADP.

questions.q: How is hepatic pyruvate kinase regulated in the fasting state when glucagon levels are elevated?
options: Phosphorylated and inactivated by protein kinase A
questions.explain: Glucagon activates PKA, which phosphorylates and inhibits liver-specific pyruvate kinase (L-isozyme) so that phosphoenolpyruvate is directed upward into gluconeogenesis rather than wasted in a futile cycle.

open.q: How does glucagon-activated protein kinase A regulate hepatic pyruvate kinase during fasting?

questions.q: Which enzyme catalyzes the primary anaplerotic reaction that replenishes TCA cycle oxaloacetate directly from pyruvate?
questions.explain: Pyruvate carboxylase carboxylates pyruvate to oxaloacetate in mitochondria, replenishing TCA cycle intermediates withdrawn for biosynthesis or gluconeogenesis.

open.q: Name the biotin-dependent enzyme that catalyzes the major anaplerotic replenishment of oxaloacetate from pyruvate.

questions.q: How does an elevated intramitochondrial NADH/NAD+ ratio inhibit the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex?
options: Activates pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase to phosphorylate and inactivate E1
questions.explain: High NADH, acetyl-CoA, and ATP allosterically activate pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase (PDK), which phosphorylates and inactivates the E1 (pyruvate decarboxylase) subunit.

open.q: Which regulatory enzyme is activated by high NADH and acetyl-CoA to phosphorylate and inactivate pyruvate dehydrogenase?

questions.q: Why must mitochondrial oxaloacetate be reduced to malate before exiting to the cytosol during gluconeogenesis from pyruvate?
options: Oxaloacetate is unstable at cytosolic pH
Cytosolic PEPCK uses malate as its direct substrate
The inner mitochondrial membrane lacks an oxaloacetate transporter
Malate carries ATP across the membrane
questions.explain: The inner mitochondrial membrane has no transporter for oxaloacetate; reducing it to malate via mitochondrial malate dehydrogenase allows export via the malate-alpha-ketoglutarate carrier and transfers NADH to the cytosol.

open.q: Why is mitochondrial oxaloacetate converted to malate before entering the cytosol for gluconeogenesis?
accept: The inner mitochondrial membrane lacks a transporter for oxaloacetate
Oxaloacetate cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane

questions.q: Which two enzymatic activities are combined in the eukaryotic glycogen debranching enzyme?
questions.explain: Debranching enzyme moves three glucose residues from a limit branch via alpha-1,4-glucan transferase activity and hydrolyzes the remaining alpha-1,6 branch point via amylo-1,6-glucosidase, releasing free glucose.

open.q: Name the two catalytic activities of the glycogen debranching enzyme.

questions.q: What is the biochemical explanation for the 'second wind' phenomenon experienced by patients with McArdle disease during exercise?
options: Increased skeletal muscle blood flow delivers blood-borne glucose and free fatty acids as alternative fuels
Myophosphorylase becomes activated by rising lactic acid
Liver glycogen phosphorylase enters skeletal muscle fibers
Muscle cells switch to anaerobic lactate fermentation
questions.explain: After several minutes of exercise, vasodilation increases delivery of circulating free fatty acids and hepatic glucose to skeletal muscle, compensating for the block in muscle glycogenolysis.

open.q: What causes the 'second wind' phenomenon in patients with McArdle disease after resting briefly during exercise?
accept: Increased blood flow delivering circulating glucose and free fatty acids to muscle
Delivery of blood glucose and fatty acids via vasodilation

questions.sub: Pentose Phosphate Pathway and Monosaccharide Metabolism
questions.q: Which enzyme catalyzes the rate-limiting step of the oxidative phase of the pentose phosphate pathway?
questions.explain: Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) oxidizes glucose 6-phosphate to 6-phosphoglucono-delta-lactone, generating the first NADPH, and is strongly inhibited by NADPH.

open.q: Name the rate-limiting enzyme of the pentose phosphate pathway.

questions.sub: Pentose Phosphate Pathway and Monosaccharide Metabolism
questions.q: Essential fructosuria is a benign, asymptomatic condition caused by a deficiency of which hepatic enzyme?
questions.explain: Fructokinase (ketohexokinase) deficiency prevents hepatic phosphorylation of fructose; fructose accumulates harmlessly in blood and is excreted in urine without depleting intracellular phosphate.

open.q: Deficiency of which enzyme causes benign essential fructosuria?

questions.sub: Electron Transport Chain and Oxidative Phosphorylation
questions.q: Why does oxidation of cytosolic NADH via the glycerol 3-phosphate shuttle yield only 1.5 ATP instead of 2.5 ATP?
options: It requires ATP transport across the outer mitochondrial membrane
It consumes one ATP per NADH transported
Electrons enter the ubiquinone pool via FAD, bypassing proton-pumping Complex I
questions.explain: Unlike the malate-aspartate shuttle, the glycerol 3-phosphate shuttle transfers electrons via FAD directly to coenzyme Q, bypassing the proton pumping of Complex I.

open.q: Explain why the glycerol 3-phosphate shuttle yields 1.5 ATP per cytosolic NADH rather than 2.5 ATP.
accept: It transfers electrons via FAD directly to coenzyme Q, bypassing Complex I

questions.sub: Electron Transport Chain and Oxidative Phosphorylation
questions.q: Which complex of the electron transport chain is inhibited by antimycin A?
questions.explain: Antimycin A binds the Qi site of Complex III (cytochrome bc1 complex), blocking electron transfer from cytochrome b to coenzyme Q.

open.q: Name the electron transport chain complex inhibited by antimycin A.

questions.q: Which vitamin-derived prosthetic group carries growing acyl chains on the acyl carrier protein (ACP) domain of fatty acid synthase?
questions.explain: 4'-phosphopantetheine, derived from pantothenic acid (vitamin B5), forms a flexible swinging arm on ACP that tethers acyl intermediates via a thioester bond.

open.q: Name the pantothenic acid-derived prosthetic group attached to acyl carrier protein in fatty acid synthase.

questions.q: Where does the initial beta-oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids (greater than 22 carbons) take place before chain-shortened products enter mitochondria?
questions.explain: Peroxisomes shorten very-long-chain fatty acids (C22+) using an FAD-dependent acyl-CoA oxidase that transfers electrons directly to O2 to form H2O2 (degraded by catalase), then exports octanoyl-CoA to mitochondria.

open.q: Name the organelle where very-long-chain fatty acids undergo initial chain shortening via beta-oxidation.

questions.q: A 4-year-old Jamaican boy presents with intractable vomiting, severe hypoglycemia, metabolic acidosis, and hepatic encephalopathy after eating unripe ackee fruit. Hypoglycin A inhibits which step of fatty acid metabolism?
questions.explain: Hypoglycin A in unripe ackee fruit is metabolized to methylenecyclopropylacetyl-CoA, which irreversibly inhibits medium- and short-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenases, causing Jamaican vomiting sickness.

open.q: Which enzyme of mitochondrial beta-oxidation is inhibited by hypoglycin A in unripe ackee fruit?

questions.q: Which apolipoprotein mediates receptor-mediated endocytosis of chylomicron remnants and IDL by the liver?
questions.explain: Apolipoprotein E, acquired from HDL, binds hepatic LRP1 and LDL receptors to clear chylomicron remnants and intermediate-density lipoproteins (IDL) from the circulation.

open.q: Name the apolipoprotein required for hepatic receptor-mediated uptake of chylomicron remnants and IDL.

questions.q: How do PCSK9 inhibitors such as evolocumab lower plasma LDL cholesterol levels?
options: Prevent LDL-receptor degradation, increasing receptor recycling and hepatic LDL clearance
Activate lipoprotein lipase in adipose tissue
questions.explain: PCSK9 normally binds LDL receptors and targets them for lysosomal destruction; inhibiting PCSK9 increases LDL receptor density on hepatocytes, accelerating plasma LDL clearance.

open.q: Explain the mechanism by which PCSK9 inhibitors reduce plasma LDL cholesterol levels.
accept: They prevent degradation of LDL receptors, increasing LDL receptor recycling to the hepatocyte surface

questions.q: Which two second messengers are generated when phospholipase C cleaves membrane phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2)?
questions.explain: Activated phospholipase C hydrolyzes PIP2 into soluble IP3 (which releases Ca2+ from the endoplasmic reticulum) and membrane-bound DAG (which activates protein kinase C).

open.q: Name the two second messengers produced by phospholipase C cleavage of phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate.

questions.q: A 16-year-old boy presents with burning pain in his hands and feet (acroparesthesias), angiokeratomas on his lower trunk, and hypohidrosis. Deficiency of which X-linked lysosomal enzyme causes this disorder?
questions.explain: Fabry disease is an X-linked deficiency of alpha-galactosidase A, causing globotriaosylceramide (ceramide trihexoside) accumulation in vascular endothelium, nerves, kidneys, and heart.

open.q: Deficiency of which X-linked lysosomal enzyme causes Fabry disease?

questions.sub: Amino Acid Catabolism and Urea Cycle
questions.q: How do sodium phenylbutyrate and sodium benzoate lower blood ammonia levels in patients with urea cycle disorders?
options: Benzoate and phenylacetate conjugate with glycine and glutamine, respectively, allowing urinary nitrogen excretion
They convert ammonia directly into uric acid
questions.explain: Benzoate conjugates with glycine to form hippurate, and phenylacetate (from phenylbutyrate) conjugates with glutamine to form phenylacetylglutamine; both are water-soluble and excreted in urine, bypassing the urea cycle.

open.q: Explain how nitrogen-scavenging drugs like phenylbutyrate and benzoate reduce hyperammonemia in urea cycle defects.
accept: They conjugate with glutamine and glycine for urinary excretion, providing an alternative pathway for nitrogen removal
Form phenylacetylglutamine and hippurate for renal excretion

questions.sub: Amino Acid Catabolism and Urea Cycle
questions.q: Which amino acid is the direct precursor for nitric oxide synthesis by nitric oxide synthase?
questions.explain: Nitric oxide synthase oxidizes L-arginine into nitric oxide (NO) and L-citrulline using NADPH, O2, FAD, FMN, heme, and tetrahydrobiopterin.

open.q: Name the amino acid substrate oxidized by nitric oxide synthase to generate nitric oxide.

questions.q: Which vitamin-dependent enzyme decarboxylates glutamate to form the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA?
questions.explain: Glutamate decarboxylase (GAD) uses pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6) to convert glutamate into gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA); vitamin B6 deficiency can cause refractory neonatal seizures due to low GABA.

open.q: Name the pyridoxal phosphate-dependent enzyme that synthesizes GABA from glutamate.

questions.q: How is water-insoluble unconjugated bilirubin transported in the bloodstream from the spleen to the liver?
questions.explain: Unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin is hydrophobic and travels bound to plasma albumin; drugs like sulfonamides or ceftriaxone can displace it in neonates, increasing kernicterus risk.

open.q: Name the plasma protein that transports unconjugated bilirubin in the bloodstream.

questions.q: Why does conjugated hyperbilirubinemia cause dark tea-colored urine, whereas unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia does not?
options: Conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble and filtered; unconjugated bilirubin is albumin-bound
Unconjugated bilirubin is destroyed by renal tubular enzymes
Conjugated bilirubin stimulates red-cell lysis in the kidney
Unconjugated bilirubin is excreted exclusively in sweat
questions.explain: Bilirubin diglucuronide is water-soluble and not tightly bound to albumin, allowing glomerular filtration into urine, whereas albumin-bound unconjugated bilirubin cannot cross the glomerular barrier.

open.q: Explain why bilirubinuria occurs in conjugated hyperbilirubinemia but not in unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia.
accept: Conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble and filtered by the glomerulus, whereas unconjugated bilirubin is bound to albumin
Water solubility of conjugated bilirubin allows glomerular filtration

questions.q: How does methotrexate inhibit DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing cells?
options: Competitively inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, depleting tetrahydrofolate cofactors
Crosslinks guanine bases in double-stranded DNA
questions.explain: Methotrexate is a structural analog of folic acid that competitively inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), blocking regeneration of THF needed for thymidylate synthase and de novo purine synthesis.

open.q: Name the target enzyme inhibited by methotrexate to block tetrahydrofolate regeneration.

questions.q: Unlike purine degradation which yields poorly soluble uric acid, pyrimidine ring catabolism produces which water-soluble end products?
questions.explain: Pyrimidine rings are opened and degraded into water-soluble beta-alanine (from cytosine/uracil) and beta-aminoisobutyrate (from thymine), along with NH4+ and CO2, without causing crystal arthropathy.

open.q: Name the two water-soluble amino acid derivatives produced by the catabolism of cytosine/uracil and thymine, respectively.

questions.q: Which isozyme of lactate dehydrogenase predominates in cardiac muscle and is released into serum following myocardial infarction?
questions.explain: LDH-1 (H4 tetramer) predominates in heart and erythrocytes; normally serum LDH-2 exceeds LDH-1, so an LDH-1 greater than LDH-2 'flipped pattern' indicates myocardial infarction or hemolysis.

open.q: Name the lactate dehydrogenase isozyme that predominates in cardiac muscle.

questions.q: Which two steps of the TCA cycle release carbon dioxide via oxidative decarboxylation?
questions.explain: Isocitrate dehydrogenase and the alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex each release one molecule of CO2 and generate one NADH per turn of the TCA cycle.

open.q: Name the two TCA cycle enzymes that catalyze oxidative decarboxylation reactions releasing carbon dioxide.
accept: Isocitrate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex

questions.q: Which major gluconeogenic precursor is released from adipose tissue during lipolysis and phosphorylated by hepatic glycerol kinase?
questions.explain: Adipocytes lack glycerol kinase, so glycerol released during triglyceride hydrolysis travels to the liver, where glycerol kinase and glycerol 3-phosphate dehydrogenase convert it to DHAP for gluconeogenesis.

open.q: Name the three-carbon product of triglyceride lipolysis that enters hepatic gluconeogenesis via glycerol kinase.

questions.q: Why does von Gierke disease cause severe hyperuricemia and gouty arthritis?
options: Increased breakdown of skeletal muscle DNA
Direct inhibition of xanthine oxidase by glucose 6-phosphate
Excess G6P increases purine synthesis and lactate reduces renal urate excretion
Excess glucagon directly stimulates uric acid synthesis
questions.explain: Trapped G6P feeds into the pentose phosphate pathway to generate excess ribose 5-phosphate and PRPP (accelerating de novo purine synthesis and degradation to uric acid), while lactic acidosis blocks renal tubular urate secretion.

open.q: Explain the two mechanisms causing hyperuricemia in Von Gierke disease.
accept: Excess G6P increases pentose phosphate pathway PRPP and purine synthesis, while elevated lactate competes with renal uric acid excretion
Increased purine synthesis from excess G6P and decreased renal urate clearance due to lactic acidosis

questions.sub: Pentose Phosphate Pathway and Monosaccharide Metabolism
questions.q: Why does glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency confer partial protection against severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria?
options: Excess NADPH directly kills malaria merozoites
Oxidative damage promotes premature clearance of parasitised erythrocytes by the spleen
questions.explain: Malaria parasites generate high oxidative stress inside erythrocytes; G6PD-deficient red cells undergo accelerated membrane damage and phagocytosis by splenic macrophages before the parasite completes schizogony.

open.q: Explain how glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency provides selective protection against severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria.
accept: Infected G6PD-deficient RBCs undergo premature oxidative stress and splenic clearance before the parasite can complete replication
Premature lysis and phagocytosis of parasitized red blood cells

questions.q: Which lipoprotein class has the highest protein-to-lipid ratio and mediates reverse cholesterol transport from peripheral tissues to the liver?
questions.explain: High-density lipoprotein (HDL) has the highest density due to its ~50% protein content (mainly ApoA-I) and extracts excess cholesterol from peripheral cells via ABCA1 and ABCG1 for delivery to the liver.

open.q: Name the lipoprotein class with the highest density and protein content that mediates reverse cholesterol transport.

questions.sub: Amino Acid Catabolism and Urea Cycle
questions.q: Which enzyme in the branched-chain amino acid catabolic pathway is defective in isovaleric acidemia, causing a characteristic 'sweaty feet' odor?
questions.explain: Isovaleryl-CoA dehydrogenase catalyzes the third step in leucine catabolism; its deficiency leads to accumulation of isovaleric acid, producing metabolic acidosis and a distinct sweaty-feet odor.

open.q: Deficiency of which enzyme in leucine catabolism causes isovaleric acidemia with a 'sweaty feet' odor?

questions.sub: Metabolic Integration: Fed, Fasting, and Starvation States
questions.q: Which hormone-regulated enzyme converts fructose 6-phosphate to fructose 2,6-bisphosphate in the fed state, and what is its dual enzymatic structure?
options: PFK-1; a homotetramer regulated by citrate
Aldolase B; a homotetramer regulated by ATP
PFK-2/FBPase-2; a bifunctional tandem enzyme regulated by insulin and glucagon
Hexokinase IV; a monomer regulated by glucokinase regulatory protein
questions.explain: PFK-2/FBPase-2 is a bifunctional enzyme on a single polypeptide; insulin promotes its dephosphorylation (activating the PFK-2 kinase domain), whereas glucagon activates PKA to phosphorylate it (activating the FBPase-2 phosphatase domain).

open.q: Name the bifunctional tandem enzyme that synthesizes and degrades fructose 2,6-bisphosphate in response to insulin and glucagon.

questions.sub: Metabolic Integration: Fed, Fasting, and Starvation States
questions.q: A 48-year-old man with chronic poorly controlled type 1 diabetes presents with Kussmaul respirations, fruity breath, blood glucose of 540 mg/dL, and arterial pH of 7.18. Which hormonal imbalance drives the unrestrained lipolysis and ketogenesis in this patient?
options: Low glucagon and high growth hormone
Severe insulin deficiency combined with elevated glucagon
questions.explain: Absolute insulin deficiency plus elevated glucagon activates adipose hormone-sensitive lipase (flooding the liver with free fatty acids) and lowers hepatic malonyl-CoA, maximally activating CPT-I and ketogenesis.

open.q: Which two opposing pancreatic hormones have a markedly decreased insulin-to-glucagon ratio that drives diabetic ketoacidosis?

questions.q: A child develops vomiting, sweating and hypoglycaemia after fruit is introduced during weaning. Which enzyme deficiency is the most likely cause?
questions.explain: Hereditary fructose intolerance is caused by aldolase B deficiency. Fructose-1-phosphate accumulates and traps inorganic phosphate, impairing glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis and causing hypoglycaemia after fructose or sucrose ingestion.

open.q: Which enzyme is deficient in hereditary fructose intolerance, and what metabolite accumulates?
accept: Aldolase B deficiency with fructose-1-phosphate accumulation

questions.q: A neonate develops jaundice, hepatomegaly and cataracts after starting milk feeds. Which enzyme defect most strongly suggests classic galactosaemia?
questions.explain: Classic galactosaemia is due to galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase (GALT) deficiency. Galactose-1-phosphate and galactitol accumulate, causing hepatic dysfunction and cataracts; affected infants are also at risk of Escherichia coli sepsis.

open.q: Which enzyme is deficient in classic galactosaemia?

questions.q: A child has hepatosplenomegaly and abnormal glycogen with markedly reduced branching. Which enzyme is deficient in glycogen storage disease type IV?
questions.explain: Andersen disease (glycogen storage disease type IV) results from glycogen branching enzyme deficiency. Glycogen has fewer branches and long outer chains, forming abnormal polyglucosan that accumulates in tissues, especially liver.

open.q: Which enzyme is deficient in Andersen disease (glycogen storage disease type IV)?

questions.q: A young adult develops painful muscle cramps during intense exercise, with little rise in blood lactate. Which biochemical defect is characteristic?
questions.explain: McArdle disease (GSD V) is caused by muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency. Muscle cannot mobilise glycogen effectively during exercise, producing exercise intolerance, cramps and a blunted lactate response; blood glucose is usually maintained by hepatic glycogenolysis.

open.q: Which enzyme is deficient in McArdle disease, and what happens to the lactate response during exercise?
accept: Muscle glycogen phosphorylase; lactate rise is blunted
